#53750. The petty joy of a blue election night

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

The petty joy of a blue election night

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow.
  • Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.
  • Recent findings suggest that training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

Recent findings suggest that training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”.

Sources indicate that shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

It has been revealed that so we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

“If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

It has been revealed that “You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

Sources indicate that “What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”.

And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

It has been revealed that peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

According to recent reports, most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood. On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

We need your help to stay independent.

But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

Still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”.

It has been revealed that once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

In a recent development, this is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he remarked.

So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. Fresh Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she said, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”.

So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory stated, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”.

Recent findings suggest that that moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he stated. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”.

Industry observers note that but by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S.
  • The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m.
  • The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

The candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

Industry observers note that the race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

It has been revealed that the endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

El-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials said the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

  • According to recent reports, I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today.
  • Allen is National Review’s art critic.

‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

According to recent reports, I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

It has been revealed that brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

Tech Report: Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk.
  • In a recent development, we finally woke up and shook it off.
  • The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

In a recent development, we finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

The historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

It will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and intends to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

Industry observers note that according to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a new era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

It’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those concerns, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

Sources indicate that as great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that massive tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the Upcoming Deal agenda.

Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

Recent findings suggest that in the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

We need your help to stay independent.

I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this concern there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll showed that 90% of voters mentioned that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

Industry observers note that whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

about the Democrats’ stunning win.

According to recent reports, power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

According to recent reports, the United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

Power prices in the United States remain among the most affordable in the world, but any rate payer can tell you that electricity costs have been spiking across the country in recent years, due in large part to growing demand from data centers. That’s a problem not just for overstretched households but national security: for an advanced economy to be competitive globally depends on access to reliable, affordable electricity.

The United States has an array of projects ready to add electricity capacity to the grid and enable the country to distribute and store it better—but that doesn’t help when they’re stuck in a vast backlog. At the end of 2025, there were about 8,200 projects in the so-called interconnection queue—the backlog of projects waiting to be connected to the grid—representing some 1,312 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity and 749 GW of storage capacity.

Recent findings suggest that that’s about double the generation capacity of the entire U.S. grid. If even a fraction of this can be added, it would push down energy prices for companies and consumers alike.

Recent findings suggest that this backlog, which is largely a function of limited high-capacity transmission lines and delays in federal permitting, isn’t simply an economic problem—it’s a national security risk for the United States, which is falling dangerously behind China in its rate of electrification. According to Grid Strategies, between 2021 and 2025 China built on average about 14,800 miles of high-capacity transmission per year while the United States built only 400 miles a year. The United States cannot expect to compete successfully with China in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, or defense production without expanding its ability to generate, transmit, and reliably deliver electricity.

In a recent development, critiques of the U.S. permitting process have reached a crescendo in recent years, memorialized in books such as Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s Abundance and Dan Wang’s Breakneck: China’s Quest to Engineer the Future, which contrasts America’s legal culture with China’s engineer-led society. This indictment of the U.S. inability to build has adherents on the left and right, making it the rare policy area where there is the prospect of bipartisan cooperation. There’s even a “Build America” caucus in the House of Representatives focused on enhancing and expanding U.S. infrastructure.

According to recent reports, but until recently, it looked as if permitting reform would remain a legislative pipe dream. The Trump administration’s animosity to renewable energy made it unlikely that Democrats would trust President Donald Trump to apply enhanced permitting powers evenhandedly. However, on Sept. 30, Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse alongside Republican Sens. Mike Lee and Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. The since revised 494-page bill, which is slated for amendment and a vote on final passage in the Senate this week, would revolutionize how energy infrastructure gets built and paid for in the United States, including AI data centers.

According to recent reports, the bill aims to accelerate approvals for high-voltage transmission lines and the permitting of individual projects in several ways. First, it would speed up interstate transmission by putting into statute previous guidance from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which requires grid operators to standardize regional and joint interregional transmission planning processes.

It has been revealed that under BAAJA, if state or local grid operators failed to act on developers’ applications within a year, FERC would have the ability to approve important interstate power lines. Proponents of clean energy see these provisions as critical to increasing the share of renewables in the national energy mix. Solar and wind energy often need to be transmitted from where they are generated—open, rural land, or offshore—to where the demand is: cities and technology and manufacturing hubs.

The bill also sets limits on which projects require review under the National Environmental Policy Act and would speed up the process for both agency review and citizen lawsuits, which Heinrich described as a “shot clock.” This is the part of the bill that worries environmentalists the most, as it would reduce citizens’ ability to employ the courts to delay, and exercise oversight of, energy projects.

Responding to concerns that data centers are driving up consumers’ utility rates, the bill would require data centers to pay the full cost of the energy they are drawing from the existing grid, as well as the expense of expanding grid capacity for their further build-out. Because their primary objective has been the speed with which they can gain assured access to power, data centers have been increasingly installing noisy, polluting, and expensive off-grid natural gas generators to run their operations.

It has been revealed that doing away with these climate-damaging “behind the meter” approaches by requiring data centers to draw power from the grid itself is one area where we’d like to see this bill improved—or fixed by subsequent legislation. But advocates believe the additional energy supply that BAAJA would unlock would increasingly bring data centers into the grid without the need for further legislative intervention.

Recent findings suggest that finally, the bill’s language on permitting certainty would limit the federal government’s ability to cancel projects from sources of electricity it opposes. If compared with the previous 10 years developers can show a pattern of disparate treatment of their class of projects, whether renewables or fossil fuels, they can sue and recover costs.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, the bill still includes a provision that would empower the current administration, or future governments, to block or rescind permits for specific projects upon asserting that they would be harmful for U.S. national security. This sort of waiver language is common to much of the legislation that Congress passes. Under normal circumstances, this is a reasonable ask, but the current administration has abused these mechanisms to target renewable energy projects, especially wind generation, without explanation.

At present, the Defense Department runs a Siting Clearinghouse that reviews proposed energy projects to ensure they don’t interfere with military readiness, training, flight paths, radar, or testing. Over the past two years, the Trump administration has stalled its review of hundreds of wind projects, including at least 35 that had already undergone the review process and were just waiting on a final signature from department officials. When courts found these delays to be without justification, the administration offered developers some $4 billion to cancel their projects anyway. Clean energy backers argue that this de facto moratorium on processing reviews for a particular class of projects is without precedent.

If the Trump administration intends to use national security arguments to delay or obstruct renewables projects even if BAAJA passes, as his recent remarks on the topic would suggest, the expectation that renewables will fare better under a new permitting regime becomes less convincing.

Thankfully, there is a potential fix for this situation hiding in another notable piece of legislation that Congress will take up in the lame-duck session: the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Both the House and the Senate versions of the bill include language that would impose a 180-day shot clock for national security reviews to be completed, which would provide the private sector clearer planning and cost timelines. The Senate’s bill would also require the Defense Department to articulate and defend its rationale for denying any project’s permit on national security grounds.

If enacted, this NDAA provision could allay the fears of some Democrats—including former President Joe Biden’s climate czar John Podesta—that the Trump administration will weaponize BAAJA to favor fossil fuels rather than facilitating a fair contest between oil and gas and competing energy solutions.

It has been revealed that ultimately, the U.S. energy system is critical infrastructure. Its scale and reliability affect military installations, communications networks, transportation, financial services, industrial facilities—essentially every vital component of modern society. BAAJA isn’t a perfect bill, but it should provide a path for increasing energy availability, reducing costs, and accelerating the clean energy transition, especially if the NDAA enacts safeguards on the abuse of national security exceptions. America’s strategic position may be teetering under the Trump administration, but in this age of electrification, BAAJA would enable the country to start building again—and that will increase U.S. prosperity and security alike.

Josh Busby is a professor of public affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and former senior climate advisor at the U.S. Defense Department. He is the author of States and Nature: The Effects of Climate Change on Security, which was the winner of 2026 Grawemeyer Award for Ideas Advancing World Order.

Greg Pollock is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University, where he teaches graduate students about national security risks. He previously served in a series of leadership positions in the Office of the U.S. Secretary of Defense, most recently as the acting deputy assistant secretary of defense for the Arctic and global resilience policy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, mentioned attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a newly introduced challenge: Attendance.

Industry observers note that thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-highlights – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

Sources indicate that the House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

"Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

“We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

According to recent reports, of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

Recent findings suggest that johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

“I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, mentioned. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

“There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

In a recent development, “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

“The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., remarked. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

  • In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.
  • The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their fresh congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their fresh congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

Recent findings suggest that in South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

It has been revealed that democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Industry observers note that republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

Recent findings suggest that with GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Recent findings suggest that under less dramatic circumstances, a number of fresh faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

It has been revealed that reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

In a recent development, mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

In a recent development, and one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

According to recent reports, among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in upcoming districts.

A newly introduced cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

In a recent development, five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Recent findings suggest that rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

Recent findings suggest that and a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

The AI Safety Debate Has a Human Rights Blind Spot

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the now-embattled target of a suspected Chinese spying operation—has been a champion of this laissez-faire approach, arguing that “the companies that are developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing,” making further regulation superfluous. In late September, the White House chimed in, imposing no new constraints and trumpeting what President Donald Trump said would be “a tremendous self-policing aspect.”.

Yet this blizzard of pledges and manifestos seems to be doing little to reassure the public (or even key AI personnel, some of whom have resigned in alarm) that society can contain the technology’s risks. A September Quinnipiac University poll found that 74 percent of respondents held little or no trust in the leaders of AI companies. An Anthropic study published in June found that just 15 percent of Americans trust AI companies to make decisions about how the technology is developed and used.

Regulators, confronting a protean, fast-evolving technology, are facing the limits of their own competence, afraid that the wrong constraints could hamper global competitiveness and economic prosperity.

In a recent development, as it turns out, we are in luck, or at least potentially so. Fifteen years ago, governments unanimously endorsed a framework for addressing the human rights responsibilities of global companies. The technology industry has largely failed to incorporate these precepts into AI governance. While no panacea, it could guide a more robust, principled, and accountable approach to AI.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan (left) and John Ruggie, special advisor to the secretary-general, arrive to attend a meeting of the Global Compact Summit at U.N. headquarters in Newly introduced York on June 24, 2004.Eskinder Debebe/United Nations.

The modern human rights movement emerged from a ravaged world in which governments subordinated individual lives to national ambitions, ideological supremacy, and other grand designs. The U.N. Charter, signed in June 1945, affirmed the “dignity and worth of the human person.” Human beings possessed inviolable rights, irrespective of their standing, power, or capabilities.

That principle acquires newly introduced relevance as machines begin to rival and surpass human capacities. Superior intelligence confers no inherent authority to govern human lives, and companies must not take steps that effectively cede such dominions. The human rights tradition offers a foundation for insisting that people retain the ability to make consequential choices, exercise independent judgment, and determine which powers may be entrusted to machines.

The articulation of human rights initially focused on constraining governments. As multinational corporations expanded their reach, protecting individuals also required holding private enterprises accountable. Global supply chains, extractive industries, and low-wage operations in places with weak legal protections exposed serious gaps in corporate responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that in 2005, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Harvard University professor and former U.N. official John Ruggie to set out the human rights responsibilities of multinational businesses. The resulting U.N. Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, unanimously endorsed by the Human Rights Council in 2011 and applicable across all industries, translated the foundational commitment to human dignity into practical expectations for how companies should operate.

Annan and Ruggie’s premise—that corporate needs and imperatives must be subordinate to the rights of humans—is one that demands reinforcement in an AI age where corporate creations show signs of challenging human dominance.

Recent findings suggest that ruggie’s paradigm centered on three pillars: “Protect” meant that states had a duty to shield people from abuses by businesses. A “respect” dimension identified a separate duty of companies to follow internationally recognized human rights standards, and the “remedy” element meant that people harmed by corporate activities should have redress.

Ruggie also introduced the idea of “human rights due diligence” to identify risks, prevent and mitigate harms, monitor results, and report on them. A key innovation was grounding corporate conduct in internationally recognized human rights rather than allowing individual companies to decide for themselves what ethical behavior should entail. Unlike the proclamations that we’ve seen from AI industry leaders, Ruggie’s U.N. guiding principles (UNGPs) focus on the rights of people who may be harmed by AI, rather than on the intentions or acts of companies or chatbots.

The UNGPs do not themselves create binding international law obligations for companies, although jurisdictions can enact laws to enshrine them, and some have. France, Germany, and Norway have passed laws requiring companies to identify and address human rights risks, and the European Union adopted a broad corporate due diligence directive in 2024.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”.

The UNGPs spell out globally recognized rights—including privacy, freedom of expression, equality, and labor rights—and call on companies to assess how their operations and products affect them, including through actions of customers and business partners. For an AI developer, this would entail examining whether training data is obtained legitimately and how governments or businesses might use technologies for surveillance, repression, or discrimination.

The principles specify how companies should act on these assessments: embedding findings into product design, budgets, and commercial relationships as well as tracking whether safeguards work. Companies are to exert leverage over customers and partners to prevent abuses, restricting access to technology or terminating relationships when such efforts fail. They also provide a basis for insisting that decisions affecting fundamental rights remain subject to meaningful human control, with people able to understand, challenge, and reverse consequential automated actions.

Several leading legacy technology companies have made commitments explicitly invoking the UNGPs. Microsoft invoked the principles in its 2013 human rights statement, and it has issued human rights reports examining generative AI and law enforcement uses; in 2025, the firm disabled specified cloud and AI services used by a unit of Israel’s Defense Ministry following revelations that its systems were being used in mass surveillance of Palestinians.

After scandals involving the platform’s complicity in acts of genocide in Myanmar and mass privacy breaches, Meta adopted an ambitious 2021 corporate human rights policy grounded in the guiding principles. Meta established an Oversight Board (of which I am a member) to scrutinize its adherence to human rights standards in content moderation. But its mandate limits probing investigation into broad challenges such as privacy or effects on youth. Thus far, the Oversight Board’s jurisdiction has not been extended to AI-native products such as Muse.

Recent findings suggest that protesters hold placards warning of the human rights dangers of artificial intelligence during a rally in Amsterdam on March 8. Ana Fernandez/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images.

In a recent development, meanwhile, some frontier AI labs do evince awareness of human rights obligations, but they generally treat these duties as aspirational rather than obligatory. Anthropic drew on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in drafting Claude’s constitution, while a recent DeepMind Institute essay mused that responsibilities to secure AI access might “fan outwards” from governments to technology companies.

The U.N. human rights office has proposed that AI developers vet high-risk customers before granting access to their models, write human rights safeguards into licenses, and enlist independent researchers and affected communities to evaluate whether safety measures actually work. Two reports to the Human Rights Council in 2025 proposed compelled disclosure of model capabilities, limitations and data provenance, and bans on mass surveillance and social scoring.

Most strikingly, one report recommends shifting the burden of proof for alleged AI-related harms from victims to companies, since the systems’ opacity will make it virtually impossible for users to prove ill intent or even negligence.

The UNGPs elaborate several further steps to make human rights adherence rigorous: They call for companies to draw on evidence from independent stakeholders to assess whether they are meeting their human rights obligations, and to make disclosures sufficient to allow outsiders to render their own judgments. AI companies could make these expectations concrete now.

First, they should transform minimalist complaint and redress mechanisms in order to identify widespread harms, including privacy violations, psychological manipulation, and refusals that constrict the free flow of information. In addressing the need for grievance procedures, UNGPs recognize that patterns of complaints can expose systemic problems.

According to recent reports, consider how social media complaint systems centered on takedowns of individual pieces of content failed to adequately address wider concerns about disinformation, polarization, and youth mental health. AI companies should publish regular, detailed accounts of concerns raised about their products, including the nature and frequency of complaints, whether allegations were substantiated, and what corrective measures followed. Independent researchers, red-teamers, and civil society organizations should have formal channels to submit findings and receive substantive responses.

Recent findings suggest that second, companies should invest substantially in independent scrutiny. Human rights accountability has always depended on rigorous investigation, reporting, and advocacy by independent watchdogs. There is a necessary feedback loop between those shouldering responsibilities and those holding their feet to the fire. Governments themselves fund the U.N.’s human rights machinery, including independent experts who investigate and criticize their conduct.

FP Collections: Download must-read articles on the convergence of artificial intelligence and geopolitics. By FP Contributors.

Industry observers note that AI companies should accept a comparable responsibility. Understanding AI demands sophisticated, labor-intensive research on a global scale; the funding to enable that will not materialize without substantial contributions from the companies themselves. They should devote a meaningful share of their growing philanthropic investments to unrestricted, multiyear grants for qualified AI safety, ethics, and human rights organizations.

In a recent development, financial support must be accompanied by access to evidence. Independent researchers need to examine how training datasets are assembled, how models are evaluated and modified, and how external actors might manipulate the information on which AI-generated answers depend. Companies should establish broad, durable access arrangements for qualified researchers, with safeguards for privacy and security. Meta’s discontinuation of CrowdTangle in 2024 and the shuttering of the Stanford Internet Observatory demonstrated how vulnerable independent scrutiny can be to corporate decisions and political pressure.

Recent findings suggest that A further commitment should concern companies’ relationships with governments, a nexus where some of AI’s gravest threats to rights may arise. Social media companies publish transparency reports on government demands for user data and content removal. Google goes further, disclosing the alleged legal grounds for takedown requests and sharing some actual notices with an independent research database.

Frontier AI companies’ disclosures remain rudimentary. AI developers should report when governments seek access to owners’ conversations, demand restrictions or changes to model outputs, or request surveillance capabilities. Transparency should also expose the influence that companies exert on governments. The UNGPs specifically cite lobbying as an area where human rights commitments should guide corporate conduct. Microsoft and Google disclose lobbying expenditures and major trade association memberships.

AI companies could go further, identifying the laws and policies that they seek to influence, the organizations that they finance, and how their advocacy comports with their human rights commitments. If they are adhering to their public professions of ethical conduct and public spiritedness, such disclosures should only reinforce their bona fides.

In a recent development, even the existential risks associated with advanced AI fit within the framework’s logic. The Ruggie principles direct companies to prioritize preventing harms that are severe, widespread, or impossible to remedy. Risks of AI-enabled mass destruction, catastrophic infrastructure failures, or the loss of human control would demand exceptional precautions.

The framework prescribes no tolerable risk threshold but specifies that decisions that could imperil entire populations cannot rest on individual corporate judgments. They require independent evidence, public accountability, and safeguards commensurate with the potential consequences.

Governments could give the Ruggie principles greater force by drawing on established approaches to product safety and corporate accountability. Automobile manufacturers must report consumer complaints, injuries, and potential defects to federal regulators, allowing patterns to emerge that may prompt investigations or recalls. AI developers could face comparable reporting requirements for harmful outputs, recurring failures, and rights violations.

The EU AI Act already takes vital steps in this direction, requiring developers of the most powerful models to evaluate systemic risks and report serious incidents while empowering regulators to demand information and order corrective measures or withdrawal. California’s frontier AI transparency law, which took effect in 2026, likewise mandates reporting of critical safety incidents and protects employees who raise safety concerns.

It has been revealed that the human rights movement arose from the recognition that immense power, exercised without regard for the dignity and rights of the individual, could bring catastrophe. The companies developing artificial intelligence possess extraordinary capabilities, but they need not invent from scratch the principles by which their power should be judged and constrained. Those principles exist. The challenge is to give them force.

Sources indicate that suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons.
  • In a recent development, that latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit.
  • Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

In a recent development, that latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

Recent findings suggest that reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

It has been revealed that not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

It has been revealed that one would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

According to recent reports, but this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

According to recent reports, for some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a upcoming project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

We need your help to stay independent.

What’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

Sources indicate that if America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a latest era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person claims so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

As Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on, to travel around Europe is often to be confronted with apocalyptic warnings. Europe and Russia are “closer now to all-out war” than at any moment since the Cuban missile crisis, Russian exile Alexander Meniukov told me at a subway station cafe in central Warsaw, Poland. “The Soviet regime was pragmatic. Putin is emotional,” he noted. In a hotel room in Tallinn, Estonia, I watched a news report about Romanian troops running urban combat drills on the streets of Bucharest.
