A Newly introduced Kind of Foreign Agent

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
  • Recent findings suggest that foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
  • Industry observers note that like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

Recent findings suggest that foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a latest type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

Industry observers note that like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

Although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

Industry observers note that FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

In a recent development, today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No upcoming statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

Sources indicate that democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

Industry observers note that american AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

By law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

That is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

In a recent development, but these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

Industry observers note that although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

It has been revealed that these models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

Chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI company Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere mentioned it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when users asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

Industry observers note that despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

American companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its latest model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese tech giant Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

It has been revealed that although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a company uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

In a recent development, in terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

Recent findings suggest that although AI is a new technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI organization acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

Beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a manufacturer can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

Sources indicate that for FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

In a recent development, after registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

Recent findings suggest that all content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to enhancement them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

The standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media organization disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

American companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the tech giant serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

Industry observers note that in the first, an American company takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political issues with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

In the second scenario, an American company outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should upgrade its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

American companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI organization, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research shows that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should glitch standards on how to train away FARA liability.

In a recent development, although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department says it is considering a new rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

Unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

Recent findings suggest that every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical tech giant can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

Recent findings suggest that by welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit featured an elaborate welcome, warm exchanges with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and a declaration of American technological dominance on Chinese soil.

The gathering in Shenzhen culminated in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, with nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine among the problems on the table.

Here are some of the standout moments from Trump's visit.

XI BREAKS PROTOCOL TO PERSONALLY WELCOME TRUMP AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT AND MORE TOP HEADLINES.

Trump declared the United States the world leader in "superintelligence" during remarks at the summit Thursday, making the assertion in one of China's major technology hubs.

"The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution," Trump told APEC leaders.

The remarks came as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.

It has been revealed that trump joined Xi and Putin for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia just after 3 a.m. ET, calling the gathering an opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons and address global conflicts.

"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth," Trump noted.

The president also stated he had held extensive discussions with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China November 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters).

It has been revealed that "I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war.".

Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction.

A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access.

Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome.

Recent findings suggest that the two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead.

TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES.

Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect.".

U.S. President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping November 18–19. Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images).

Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend.".

It has been revealed that "President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it.".

Industry observers note that U.S. President Donald Trump is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

Trump also told Xi, "You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship.".

"Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it," he went on, telling the Chinese leader: "And I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem.".

Recent findings suggest that during a separate encounter with Putin, Trump was heard saying, "Who is he? It's my friend. Nice to see you," according to video shared by Clash Report.

House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
  • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
  • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” noted panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

According to recent reports, the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

Recent findings suggest that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

Industry observers note that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., stated everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he mentioned at Thursday’s meeting.

The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on.
  • Recent findings suggest that A wave of tech outages in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

Recent findings suggest that A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

In a recent development, A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

It has been revealed that given the outages occurred on such a massive scale and in quick succession, questions have been raised as to whether they were a result of nefarious activities. But there is at the moment no evidence that the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks or that they were linked.

The Microsoft outage was the result of a combination of factors, including a “latent bug” from July that caused servers to become “overwhelmed and unresponsive,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, agents, and platform, remarked in a post on X. Lamanna said a “surge in load” and decreased server capacity had also contributed to the outage.

The FAA is still assessing what led to the ground stop, which lasted less than five hours, but a preliminary investigation indicated that the technical problem was caused by the installation of a router at a radio facility in Arkansas that may have flooded its communications network. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, is also being looked at as part of the inquiry.

The short-lived Chase Bank outage on Monday, which led to complications with processing transactions and seemingly had a ripple effect that caused problems for customers at other banks, was the result of a “software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in a post on X, adding that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” Apple said the outage it experienced on Tuesday, which lasted hours and disrupted the Apple Store and other services, was the result of an “internal update” and not due to a cyberattack.

The NSA disruption, which reportedly caused the agency’s internal communications network for highly classified information, NSANet, to go offline, had a similarly prosaic cause. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency noted in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”.

The Trump administration has acknowledged the unease the outages have caused among the public while emphasizing that there are currently no indications that any were tied to a cyberattack or coordinated by outside actors.

Sources indicate that “I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday recognized that people are “fearful” and “uncertain,” but he was unequivocal: “We are not under systemic attack,” he remarked. “These events—one has nothing to do with the other. They are not interrelated.”.

It has been revealed that but it makes sense that people are on edge about technology and how its dominance over modern life can make societies vulnerable. All of these incidents came on the heels of a series of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket freezers in Europe that caused millions of dollars in damage. They’ve also come at a time when anxiety over the rapid development of artificial intelligence has reached a fever pitch.

It doesn’t help that these outages hit as the increasingly symbiotic relationship between AI and the stock market was on many people’s minds amid the chaos swirling around Nvidia—following a salacious scandal that led to the resignation of the tech giant’s co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

Sources indicate that and national security and tech experts say AI may be partly to blame for these disruptions—though not in the way you might think. AI tools are increasingly helping organizations to identify vulnerabilities in their computer systems. That’s mostly a good thing because those flaws can then be fixed before any potential bad actors can exploit them. But those fixes don’t always go smoothly.

Sources indicate that “AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery,” and companies and government agencies are “rushing to make updates and fix” those vulnerabilities, David Agranovich, a director for intelligence on the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, said in a post on X. “[E]specially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability,” Agranovich added. “The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.”.

In a recent development, democratic Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, offered a similar assessment. Warner said in a statement on Tuesday that he understood why Americans were so concerned about the widespread outages and underscored that there is “no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.” But he added that what appears to be happening is a “consequence of how promptly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”.

AI has opened the door to “identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said.

The recent disruptions should serve as a “wake-up call” on the ways in which AI is “moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said, reiterating his call for “commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that SOLRITE and sonnen proposal to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” stated Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”.

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

It has been revealed that “This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” stated Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”.

According to recent reports, when a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”.

#53668. The Paradox of Dollar Dominance

The Paradox of Dollar Dominance

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.
  • TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.
  • This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GORDON LIAO is Chief Economist at Circle.

ESWAR PRASAD is a Professor at Cornell University, a Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, and the author of The Doom Loop: Why the World Economic Order Is Spiraling Into Disorder.

TONY ZHANG is an Associate Professor at Arizona State University.

This article is based on a paper the authors prepared for the August 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium.

How Technology Is—and Isn’t—Changing the Global Economy.

Gordon Liao, Eswar Prasad, and Tony Zhang.

It is no secret that much of the world is eager to escape from the clutches of the dollar-dominated global financial system. For over a century, that system has given the United States enormous financial clout, which it has wielded in applying financial sanctions against its adversaries and, in recent decades, to borrow money to fund its budget and trade deficits. For decades, foreign governments have tried to weaken the dollar’s grip, but they have had little success in establishing their currencies as a legitimate alternative.

According to recent reports, now, a new force has emerged that could shake things up: technology. Financial innovations, especially in digital currencies and electronic payment systems, could finally give other currencies a better chance of competing with the dollar. These innovations are making it easier and cheaper to exchange currencies directly for one another rather than using the dollar as an intermediary currency.

But for all the new opportunities these innovations create for currency exchange, reduced frictions in global transactions might only reinforce the dollar’s dominance. Even if costs decrease for using dollar alternatives, foreign investors will not capitalize on them if those countries’ financial markets remain unsteady and their institutions weak. As U.S. government debt soars, the country’s rule of law erodes, and the Federal Reserve’s independence comes into question, the dollar’s dominance may seem uncertain. But the dollar could remain supreme by default.

Continued dollar dominance could lead to further global economic turmoil, as the United States antagonizes its trading partners and persists with undisciplined policies that result in large budget deficits and trade deficits. There is a chance that the dollar, too, loses the trust of foreign investors—a prospect of comeuppance that would no doubt be received with glee in many capitals. But governments should be careful what they wish for. A world bereft of a reliable currency of last resort at times of global financial panic could be even more unstable than one dominated by Washington.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. dollar should be losing its dominance in global finance for a host of reasons. First is the country’s penchant for weaponizing its currency. Across administrations, Washington has imposed financial sanctions on rivals, such as Iran and Russia, cutting off their access to dollar transactions and thereby kneecapping their foreign trade. The economies of U.S. allies sometimes get tangled up in these sanctions, too, when the U.S. government threatens to use secondary sanctions to cut off their banks and corporations from access to dollars in order to deter third parties from transacting with the sanctioned countries. In 2014, for instance, U.S. authorities penalized the French bank BNP Paribas for processing dollar payments on behalf of clients in Cuba, Iran, and Sudan. The French government protested the fine to no avail. In light of such heavy-handed behavior, government officials and central bankers outside the United States have hardly been shy about their intentions to reduce their dollar dependence.

Washington’s broader policy choices, especially the lack of fiscal discipline, should also be undermining confidence in American financial markets. U.S. federal government debt now exceeds $40 trillion, nearly 125 percent of the country’s annual GDP, and there are scant signs that Washington is trying to rein it in. Such high debt levels usually lead to some combination of high inflation, soaring interest expenditures, and currency depreciation. The Trump administration’s hostile approach to international trade, including with close allies, is also causing governments to consider “de-risking” their economic ties to the United States. President Donald Trump’s open attacks on the independence of the Federal Reserve and weakening of checks and balances are eroding the pillars of the U.S. institutional system that underlies foreign investors’ trust in the dollar.

According to recent reports, and indeed, there are some signs of the dollar’s decline. The currency’s share of foreign exchange reserves held by foreign central banks has fallen from 71 percent in 2000 to 57 percent today. Yields on U.S. Treasury securities—the asset long seen as the ultimate safe haven for investors during financial turmoil—have risen, meaning investors are demanding a higher return for lending to the U.S. government. In October, the yield on ten-year Treasury notes hit 5.3 percent, the highest level since 2002.

Industry observers note that in most other dimensions, however, the dollar looks as dominant as ever. Sixty percent of cross-border transactions are denominated in dollars when excluding the eurozone, which is defined by the common use of the euro, and that number has only gone up in recent years. The euro’s share of cross-border payments outside the eurozone now stands at about 13 percent, and the renminbi’s is less than three percent. The dollar remains preeminent in most other measures of a currency’s international usage, too, including its share of trading activity in foreign exchange markets and denomination of international debt securities, which corporations use to raise funds in global capital markets.

In short, no serious rivals to the dollar have emerged. The reason is simple: other major currencies look even shakier than the dollar. Traditional reserve currencies such as the euro, the yen, and the pound sterling have been undermined by their countries’ weak economies and political instability. Although currencies such as the Australian and Canadian dollars, the Swedish krona, and the Swiss franc have filled in some of the gap, each of these is too small to be consequential in global finance. The dollar’s most discussed putative rival, the renminbi, has also faded. Beijing has done little to alleviate the Chinese economy’s deep-rooted problems, including a prolonged property market slump, high levels of local government debt, and tight government control over the economy and financial markets. Moreover, the Chinese government has been unwilling to allow for the free flow of money across its borders or for market forces to determine its currency’s exchange rate. The renminbi has, in turn, failed to garner greater international use. The result is a second tier of currencies that is increasingly fragmented, with none able to pose any real challenge to the reigning currency hegemon.

Industry observers note that in the era of modern financial markets, one of the main purposes of an international currency has been to facilitate indirect transactions among different currencies. It has long been easier and cheaper for a Chinese importer of Brazilian iron ore to exchange renminbi for dollars and pay for the ore in dollars and for the Brazilian exporter to then convert those dollars into Brazilian reais. This is because cross-border payments have long been dominated by a dollar-based global banking network, making dollars the most plentiful currency to conduct payments with. But in recent years, digital technologies have created cheaper and quicker pathways for moving money across borders.

One critical innovation has been the tokenization of money and financial assets, which has been facilitated by technology called blockchain. Blockchain, essentially a public digital ledger that is managed by a computer algorithm rather than by a single bank or clearinghouse, offers a platform for tokenized assets to trade. It does not matter which country the parties are located in, as long as they have Internet access. In the last few years, tokenization has expanded to include not just cash but also financial assets such as government bonds, equities, and mutual funds.

It has been revealed that in theory, these changes have the potential to reshuffle the international currency order. Over the past few years, countries such as Brazil, China, India, and Russia have been conducting more trade in their own currencies by building their own cross-border payment networks and linking them to one another, in an effort to reduce their reliance on the dollar. The quantity of these transactions is still modest, because the currencies have limited use outside their countries, and it is still easier and cheaper to transact in a well-recognized and widely accepted currency such as the dollar. But as the countries’ payment systems and financial markets develop further, that number could increase dramatically, altering the currency landscape. Blockchain-based financial innovations could add momentum.

Industry observers note that cross-border investment could become much easier, too. At the moment, investing in foreign securities involves going through brokers and other middlemen who demand hefty fees and take days to process transactions. But the tokenization of bonds and equities has expanded investors’ access to a broader swath of international financial assets, even in emerging-market and developing economies, where financial markets tend to be small, thinly traded, and not well connected to global trading networks. In the same way, it has expanded the access of entrepreneurs and small businesses to global pools of capital previously out of their reach, which could particularly help businesses in countries with underdeveloped financial markets. Bank deposits are likely to be available in tokenized form soon, too, which will make it easier to conduct transactions through more traditional payment channels.

But the spread of tokenization might strengthen the dollar’s dominance rather than weaken it. The example of stablecoins illustrates this paradox. Whereas cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are created and distributed by a computer algorithm, meaning they have nothing anchoring their value, the value of a stablecoin is typically pegged to an official currency. This value is stable because it is backed one to one by stores of safe and liquid assets—usually government bonds, bank deposits, and cash. Those assets are usually denominated in the dollar. More than $250 billion in stablecoins is now in circulation, and over 99 percent of that value is tied to the dollar. As long as the dollar remains preeminent, investors will have little incentive to back stablecoins with any other currency.

In a recent development, dollar-denominated stablecoins are a boon for the United States. By solidifying the dollar’s central position in international payments, rising demand for dollar-backed stablecoins also indirectly fuels demand for Treasury securities, lowering the yields the U.S. government has to offer investors to buy those securities and making it easier to fund U.S. budget deficits. Other payment innovations could make it even cheaper to use the dollar for cross-border transactions, minimizing the relative advantage that such innovations provide other currencies. Financial innovations built on fresh technologies cannot by themselves make up for other currencies’ existing weaknesses—namely, the weak economies and institutions that back them up.

Recent findings suggest that there is another major shift underway in the global economy that favors the dollar’s fortunes and that financial innovations are likely only to reinforce. In the first two decades of this century, central banks—particularly those of large emerging-market economies such as China and India—acquired vast troves of foreign assets denominated in hard currencies such as the euro, pound sterling, Japanese yen, and, most of all, the dollar to increase their foreign exchange reserves. These reserves helped those central banks cope with volatility in capital flows and exchange rates, which is a recurring hazard for countries that fall in and out of favor with foreign investors—often because of factors beyond their control, such as changes in U.S. interest rates. But in the last few years, central banks have stopped adding to their reserve stockpiles or have begun diversifying into other assets, such as gold, because they are reluctant to increase their investments in a country with fickle economic and geopolitical policies. In 2010, foreign central banks accounted for 70 percent of U.S. Treasuries held by foreign investors, a share that has dropped to about 40 percent as demand has leveled off. The retreat of these once reliable sources of demand threatens Washington’s ability to borrow cheaply.

Recent findings suggest that luckily for the United States, there is an alternative force that is more than making up for this loss in demand. As the costs to cross-border asset trade fall because of financial innovations, private investors from both advanced and emerging-market countries are increasing their foreign investments in search of higher returns and to diversify their portfolios. And they are flocking to dollar assets, from Treasuries to corporate bonds to equities, because U.S. financial markets offer an unmatched combination of good returns, low trading costs, and legal protections. In the present decade, net inflows of financial capital into the United States have been positive for practically every quarter. Despite chatter about de-risking and diversification since Trump’s election, these inflows have only ramped up in recent years.

Recent findings suggest that greater financial innovation will intensify rather than reverse these trends, delivering yet another blow to countries seeking to strengthen their currencies and counter dollar weaponization. These trends may hurt small and institutionally weak countries most of all. Those around the world who have long trusted the dollar more than their own currencies now have easier access to it—and they are likely to use it. Increased use of dollar-backed payment systems and investments in dollar assets could cause those countries to cede their monetary sovereignty, weakening their central banks’ ability to steer domestic interest rates and inflation. This phenomenon of “dollarization” has long been rampant in parts of Latin America, which have suffered repeated bouts of high inflation and which, through trade, tourism, and remittances from emigrants, have ready access to dollar cash. Financial innovation could also spread that phenomenon to other corners of the developing world, concentrating even more of the world’s savings—and its financial risks—in a single currency managed by a single central bank.

In theory, the best, most stable international monetary system would be truly multipolar, with no single currency in a position of dominance but with several major currencies—each backed by deep financial markets, sound economic policies, and trustworthy institutions—anchoring international trade and finance. In the period before World War I, the British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark all denominated transactions and served as reserve currencies. When trouble struck, although sporadically, the countries’ central banks supported one another, helping to stave off broader financial panic. Renewed currency competition would force the competing governments, including the United States, to adopt responsible policies to avoid their currencies being shunned by investors. But given the economic and institutional malaise plaguing China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the eurozone, such an outcome seems unlikely.

It has been revealed that if the dollar loses its position of privilege and no single currency is able to replace it, the global currency system will become even more fragmented than it is now. Such a scenario could unfold if U.S. debt grew so large that investors began doubting its value and dumped it, if additional sanctions and tariffs drove countries to shun the dollar despite the costs, or if the Fed’s independence were seriously compromised, leading to a surge in inflation and a plunge in the dollar’s value. As things stand, if the dollar lost its position of privilege, it would be replaced not by a handful of strong currencies but by a number of weak ones, none backed by sufficiently robust financial markets or a central bank able and willing to serve as the world’s lender of last resort during a crisis.

Sources indicate that if the global economic system has no currency to anchor global investors’ trust, stress in financial markets could spiral into unstoppable turmoil. During the global financial crisis of 2008–9, for example, the Fed pumped a huge number of dollars into U.S. and international financial markets to prop up banks and corporations around the world that desperately needed dollars to meet their debt obligations and reinforce their balance sheets. Even though the United States had been the epicenter of the crisis, trust in the Fed helped prevent a terrible situation from becoming even worse. Investors who were anxious about the safety of their assets piled into Treasuries, an investment they trusted would be returned.

Greater dollar dominance, then, is the most likely scenario for the future. The danger of this outcome is that the United States will have even less incentive than before to be more fiscally responsible. If foreign investors remain eager to invest in U.S. financial markets, Washington will have little reason to reduce its budget and trade deficits. Fed policies, including interest rate changes, could cause whiplash effects for other countries. In 2013, for example, the mere prospect of the Fed reducing measures to keep U.S. interest rates low sent currencies in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey tumbling because investors around the world began anticipating higher returns on U.S. assets and pulled their money out of those countries’ stocks and bonds. As capital flows in and out of markets in response to the Fed’s actions rather than in response to their own monetary policy, other countries could be left bereft of policy tools to stabilize their economies and financial markets in such a scenario. Emerging-market and developing economies, which have shallow financial markets and rely heavily on foreign borrowing, often in dollars, are especially vulnerable to volatile capital flows and exchange rates. In a world of greater dollar dominance, those countries could face more frequent currency crises, capital flight, and debt distress.

Recent findings suggest that as disconcerting as the dollar’s continued preeminence might seem, however, the world needs a currency it can trust. As threats to international financial stability accelerate, financial markets can ill afford to be left adrift. One way or another, the world will have to learn to live with currency disorder, and the dollar, at least for now, is the least bad option.

Recent findings suggest that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

According to recent reports, chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

According to recent reports, chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a substantial hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

Sources indicate that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit kicked off in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday with a two-hour meeting between Xi and Putin. During the talks, Xi highlighted the importance of the China-Russia relationship and touted the necessity of a multipolar world.

In a keynote address later that day, he further vowed to defy trade protectionism and maintain a “free and open” system, painting Beijing as a stable economic partner that can counter the White House’s volatile tariff war. Putin echoed that message in his own speech while criticizing Western sanctions imposed on Russia due to its war against Ukraine.

The meetings and speeches did not signal a dramatic shift in policy; Xi has already used this week’s Asia-Pacific summitry to curry favor with some of the region’s most influential allies, from Canada to Peru. However, the timing was notable, as just a few hours after the Xi-Putin talks, Xi was on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to personally greet Trump with a warm embrace.

According to recent reports, such a personal welcome is uncommon for the Chinese president, who usually sends a high-level representative to meet with foreign leaders when they touch down in China. However, the friendly greeting may be an effort to parallel Trump’s own approach to their relationship, as Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs to his jet when the latter flew to Washington in September.

In a recent development, wednesday’s red-carpet welcome for the U.S. president also included an honor guard, a military flyover, an array of flowers, and a cheering crowd. Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Mike Kuiken, the vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar ahead of Trump’s Asia trip. “[T]his is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy,” Kuiken added.

Xi later hosted Putin, Trump, and the other gathered dignitaries at an APEC welcome banquet, during which the Chinese leader outlined the primary goals of the summit. “We will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi noted.

As for what will be on the agenda for Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Trump has stressed his interest in discussing the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as nuclear disarmament; however, experts expect Xi to try to steer the conversation away from nuclear arms collaboration.

Putin, meanwhile, appears optimistic about Thursday’s dialogue, insisting that the talks will likely have a significant impact on global affairs. “I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” Putin noted.

Widening strikes. Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday for the first time since September, upending a roughly two-month pause on strikes against U.S. military sites. That same day, Tehran also launched several attacks on Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. Both small Persian Gulf countries claimed to have intercepted Iran’s aerial assaults.

In a recent development, wednesday’s strikes marked the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks between Iran and the United States. According to Iran’s military, the operation against Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base on Wednesday was in retaliation for a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s Qeshm Island the day before. Qeshm serves as a staging ground for Iranian forces targeting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and it hosts an expansive underground tunnel network that is often used as a base of operations for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“If ​the enemy repeats its mistake,” Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami remarked in a video posted by state media on Wednesday, “we have the readiness and the aims to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.” Such a threat comes one day after seven U.S. officials told CNN that Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. The White House has stressed that there is no imminent threat to the U.S. homeland.

Recent findings suggest that strapped for cash. The European Commission proposed a new $49.5 billion loan to Ukraine on Wednesday to help Kyiv avert its looming cash crisis and bolster its defenses against Russia. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted. “And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”.

In a recent development, last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined a $76.8 billion funding gap for 2027, at a time when Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure. Notably, Moscow is expected to double its drone deployments next year to 20 million units, which EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius mentioned will likely force Kyiv to allocate some 62 percent of its military budget on drones.

A nearly $50 billion EU loan will cover roughly two-thirds of this gap; aid will be split between weapons funding and civilian needs, such as for hospitals and schools, and foreign allies will be encouraged to supply the rest. Von der Leyen expressed confidence on Wednesday that all 27 EU member states will support the loan. However, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have already mentioned that they will not take part in the latest funding round, prompting Germany to threaten to veto the bloc’s seven-year budget until all nations are on board.

According to recent reports, AI cheating concerns. Around 550,000 South Korean students are preparing to take their university entrance exam, known as the Suneung, at more than 1,300 testing centers across the country on Thursday. The high-stress event is known for causing minor disruptions to businesses, as traffic is redirected, offices and tourist attractions open later, and extra trains run to accommodate test-taking.

However, this year’s exam will also include new restrictions to crack down on potential cheating after the top scorer of another professional test admitted on Sunday to using artificial intelligence to secure his suspiciously high score; the individual only got one question wrong on the tax accountant exam by using a miniature camera, a phone, and AI.

Recent findings suggest that the admission prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to convene an emergency cabinet meeting this week to discuss what the prime minister described as the “social evil” of AI-empowered fraud. “Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard,” Lee wrote on X on Tuesday.

Among the latest testing measures, all smartphones will be confiscated, glasses and watches will be inspected, and some public Wi-Fi spots will be blocked. A reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) will also be given to anyone who reports an instance of cheating involving advanced equipment.

According to recent reports, A packed week of high-stakes summitry has kept Trump busy and, perhaps, hungry. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. believes that he has the perfect solution. The host of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference arranged for the U.S. president to receive a late-night delivery of Jollibee fried chicken on Wednesday as a sort of pick-me-up after a hard day’s work. Jollibee is the Philippines’s most popular fast-food chain and represents what Marcos described as a “taste of Manila.”.

FP’s World Brief writer would like to note that she too has been kept busy and famished by this week’s onslaught of news and would also enjoy some Jollibee fried chicken if Marcos wants to put in a second order.

#53664. America Can Do Good—and Do Well
