GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.
  • Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.
  • “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Industry observers note that ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” stated Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

In a recent development, democrats stated Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Recent findings suggest that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

Industry observers note that democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

Ueland did not give a direct response.

It has been revealed that “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he stated. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also mentioned it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

“We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

“That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

Ueland stated his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

For example, he said GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland stated he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”.

It has been revealed that sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, remarked he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

It has been revealed that paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely crucial to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” said Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, said by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

It has been revealed that he noted GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

#53636. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that LYLE J.
  • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
  • In a recent development, today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

Lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

In a recent development, today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

According to recent reports, but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

Industry observers note that there are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists unveiled that China was constructing 350 newly introduced nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-launched ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

In a recent development, then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-rolled out long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant upcoming capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan problem stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

According to recent reports, as China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

The Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

In a recent development, beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July Fresh York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby stated, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-released cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses latest warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

Industry observers note that beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an key analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as crucial, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

In a recent development, the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

Industry observers note that the Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more important, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

It has been revealed that exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

In a recent development, another crucial step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Recent findings suggest that beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

In a recent development, rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is leaving the door open to a potential 2028 presidential bid as speculation grows over her political future.

According to recent reports, "I think, right now, this election just happened. We got to work on getting results for people," Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News Digital when asked whether she was considering a presidential run in 2028.

The self-described democratic socialist also expressed a willingness to work with President Donald Trump on key legislative priorities as Democrats prepare to take control of the House following the 2026 midterm elections.

PROGRESSIVE ORG DEBUTS CAMPAIGN URGING AOC TO RUN FOR PRESIDENT WHILE PROGRESSIVES EYE SOCIALIST CANDIDATE.

It has been revealed that reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Laurel Lee, R-Fla., and Kat Cammack, R-Fla., hold a news conference with media personality Paris Hilton urging Congress to pass the DEFIANCE Act (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits Act) outside the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images).

Ocasio-Cortez, who has drawn support from the Democratic Socialists of America's (DSA) Upcoming York City chapter for a potential White House bid, emphasized her desire to advance legislation in the 120th Congress rather than focus on presidential politics.

Asked whether Democrats should work with Trump instead of prioritizing impeachment proceedings and congressional investigations, Ocasio-Cortez expressed optimism about finding common ground.

"I hope so," she told Fox News Digital.

"You know, I hope that President Trump can sign a congressional stock trading ban into law," Ocasio-Cortez continued.

The congresswoman also identified healthcare reform as a potential area for bipartisan cooperation, urging Trump to address changes to Medicaid that she warned could threaten coverage for millions of Americans.

DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo).

"I hope President Trump will be willing to work with us in really adjusting this Medicaid and confronting this Medicaid cliff that stands to kick off millions of working Americans off of their healthcare," she said.

"And so, you know, there are going to be areas where we're going to have real disagreement and real confrontation or worse," she continued.

Despite those disagreements, Ocasio-Cortez argued that lawmakers should prioritize legislation addressing Americans' immediate concerns.

"My hope is that we can prioritize the things that can actually change people's lives for the better as quickly as possible," she said.

Breaking: Is China Misreading the Moment?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
  • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

In a recent development, when U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have revealed a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

Industry observers note that the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of upcoming export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

Since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept new tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

Beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

Sources indicate that so far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his company’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And new U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

It has been revealed that although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

Recent findings suggest that prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

Beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

It has been revealed that another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the new historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

But China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

The awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

In a recent development, if diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

To keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed new export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

It has been revealed that beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end users, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing showed how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

The timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard launched water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

China has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued upcoming gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

And around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

Sources indicate that outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in Newly introduced Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

Beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set latest precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

What looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several vital questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

The United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

From the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to issue general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end users and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a fresh category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

Beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

Recent findings suggest that tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

Recent findings suggest that these headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

Sources indicate that if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

The European hometown of the man who single-handedly destroyed a U.S. military transport aircraft in an act of apparent protest has a rich history of pro-Palestinian support.

This includes the town council for Cork, Ireland, barring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from entering its city limits, citing his "illegal occupation of Palestine and bordering countries" and the continuous pro-Palestinian protests taking place every Saturday since October 2023, organized by the Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign (CPSC).

Cork’s opposition to Israel adds context to the possible motives for why Daithí O’Corráin, an Irish national, allegedly destroyed a U.S. military C-130 Hercules aircraft in April. The incident also draws attention to several anti-Israel groups that have sprung up in Ireland in recent years.

IRELAND’S ELITES HAVE FOUND THEIR FRESH RELIGION: HATING ISRAEL.

Pro-Palestinian activists from the Ireland Palestine Solidarity Campaign, supported by members of left-wing parties including People Before Profit and the Socialist Party and students, participate in the National March for Palestine from the Garden of Remembrance to O'Connell Street and Leinster House, on May 18, 2024, in Dublin, Ireland. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images).

It has been revealed that ireland’s anti-Israel foothold became international news in April when O’Corráin, a Cork native, barricaded himself inside a C-130, a U.S. military transport plane. Once inside, he tore out critical wiring, destroyed gauges, contaminated fuel tanks and even poured corrosive chemicals into the aircraft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Recent findings suggest that although his motives remain unclear, several groups from Cork interpreted his actions as a form of resistance against Israel and U.S. military interventionism.

Recent findings suggest that in one such case, a Cork business owner named Tracey Ryan launched an initiative to raise €20,000 for O’Corráin's legal defense, praising his efforts to resist "the unwanted presence of U.S. military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide.".

"We, Daithí's friends and comrades, are raising funds to support him through his court case. We would really appreciate your support & will keep you updated here on ways to support Daithí," Ryan wrote in the description of the fundraising page.

Recent findings suggest that according to her personal Facebook profile, Ryan joined a bus of pro-Palestinian activists who went to support O’Corráin at his court appearance. "Bus going to the high court to support Daithí on Thursday!!" Ryan wrote.

O’Corráin has also received support from CPSC, the Cork pro-Palestinian group.

As news of the incident spread, CPSC co-chair Anne McShane posted on her Palestinian advocacy Facebook page in support of O’Corráin, encouraging viewers to send him letters of encouragement after his incarceration.

In a recent development, "Daithi needs our support in order to keep up his morale. Letters are a lifeline for prisoners," an April 17 post read.

CPSC spearheads anti-Israel demonstrations in Cork. In addition to hosting several pro-Palestinian fundraising initiatives, the group facilitates weekly Saturday demonstrations and invites speakers. At one point, CPSC’s website featured a fundraising site for O’Corráin, but the page has since been removed.

In CPSC’s own words, the group is part of a larger pro-Palestinian movement.

"It’s not just the city. Towns across all of County Cork stand in solidarity with Palestinians, including Ballincollig, Bandon, Cobh, Charleville, Clonakilty, Fermoy, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Mitchelstown, Skibbereen and more," the group states on its website.

"Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign is a branch of the Irish Palestine Solidarity Campaign (IPSC)," it added.

As part of its sister groups’ efforts "to foster links between Palestine and Irish institutions and organizations," CPSC and IPSC have both applauded Cork’s city council efforts to promote pro-Palestinian policies.

"Well done to the Cork City Council which passed a motion … calling for the Central Bank to end the sale of Israeli bonds," one Facebook post reads.

The groups have also held Cork up as a template for Ireland’s national policy.

"We call on the Irish government to follow the example of both Dublin and Cork city councils by officially recognizing Israeli Apartheid – and acting to end any and all links to this regime," another statement reads.

For its own part, the Cork City Council has earned the support of IPSC and CPSC through a range of its official resolutions, making the town’s formal position to condemn any of Ireland’s ties to Israel.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to banning Netanyahu from entering the city's limits in a 41-8 vote in 2024, Cork’s council has flown the Palestinian flag over city hall on U.N. International Day of Solidarity and called on Ireland to ban trade from Israeli settlements.

Cork has even passed a "twinning" mechanism with the Palestinian city of Nablus — a largely symbolic partnership.

According to recent reports, thousands took to the streets in Fresh Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud. Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

In a recent development, A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

At a Diwali party last month, a young Indian researcher in her mid-20s warned me against attending a protest rally. “The police will pick you up,” she said, her eyes wide open. In a recent protest, the Delhi police had locked down major parts of the capital and cracked down on protesters. The police cut off the internet, shut down local trains in key areas, and detained thousands, including journalists. Even those hanging around weren’t spared. “Our lawyer friends who went to the protest site to help the protesters were also beaten up,” she said. “Because our friends were detained and beaten, now we fear we could be next. You could be next.”.

This is starkly different from India in 2011, when tens of thousands flocked to Jantar Mantar, a historical protest site near Delhi’s power center, for an anti-corruption demonstration. That protest paved the way for the Congress-led government’s defeat and Modi’s entry into national politics in 2014. Modi’s government, however, appears to have drawn a very different lesson about how to deal with protests.

BJP leaders suggested removing protesters because they inconvenienced passersby and businesses. That line was parroted relentlessly in TV studios. In my travels in and around Delhi, I found that message landed with certain people—mostly those who also believed the BJP’s insinuation, which came without any evidence, that protests in India were a foreign ploy to destabilize the country. Protests in India unfolded at the same time as in France and elsewhere in Europe, and this was portrayed as a sign of collaboration.

Industry observers note that however, there appears to be a pattern in how the current Indian government discredits and responds to protests. A few months ago, when Indian students marched against an exam paper leak and jobless growth, the same police thrashed the students, even firing pellet guns. Some TV anchors claimed the police were the victims.

These are unusual scenes in India, a democratic country where the right to protest is guaranteed under the constitution. India won its independence through peaceful protests against the British.

In a recent development, on Nov. 1, despite the police’s reported highhandedness, thousands of people from different parts of the country gathered for the mega protest at an alternative and government-approved protest site. By noon, as I reached Connaught Place in central Delhi, Congress workers were marching on the streets and calling for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accused Kumar of working to benefit the BJP.

But Kumar’s role and the discrepancies in electoral rolls weren’t the only reasons that pushed people to protest. Three Gen Z protesters stood in a corner, two of them wearing masks to avoid being identified by the police. “They picked up people after the protests last time, from their homes,” noted one of the masked boys. All three had joined the protests for very different reasons but the same cause—saving Indian democracy.

In a recent development, the masked boy recounted the story of how his friend, a child, was terrified for his mother’s security when Hindu-Muslim riots unfolded in Delhi early 2020. He blamed the BJP for instigating the riots. The young man standing to his left hailed from West Bengal and was furious that his grandparents, both octogenarians, were knocked off the voters list and denied the right to cast their ballot. “[The government] wanted to exclude a certain community, Bengali Muslims that they falsely say are Bangladeshis, but everyone was affected,” he noted. “They are dividing us on the basis of religion; this is not okay.”.

Mihika Omseema refused to cover up her face. She noted her parents supported her and that gave her the strength to reveal her identity and take part in protests. She said she joined to protest against growing Hindu-Muslim polarization, falling economic standards, exam paper leaks, and a whole host of other issues. In Delhi, some neighborhoods indicated a mood where parents might join their children—if not at the protest grounds, then at the ballot. A senior gentleman and an upper-caste Hindu said, “Modi will not win Delhi, no chance,” but he confessed that Modi still had many supporters in the country. An 80-kilometer ride to Meerut has been shortened from more than 3 hours to less than 2 hours via a upcoming flyover completed under Modi’s government, which has also built several other key highways linking cities in western Uttar Pradesh. Meerut, for the first time, has a fast train that reaches Delhi in less than an hour and thus expands employment potential. (Uttar Pradesh has the maximum number of electoral constituencies and plays a decisive role in forming the government in Delhi. Although central elections are still more than two years away, the state itself will go to the polls next year.).

In Meerut, I heard a different set of complaints against the BJP. Younger people acknowledged infrastructure development but said there was still no work. Only Muslims were worried about growing polarization; Hindus were more upset with slow economic growth and a demolition drive to bulldoze illegal shops and other structures. “Of course, this will affect the BJP in the elections; people are, we are, very angry with the government,” said Aditya Kumar, who sat on a stool in his emptied and recently destroyed shop in a market where rubble had still not been cleared. He sold nuts, bolts, and other construction material. “The structures were illegal, but there is no other employment, so what were we supposed to do?” he said, highlighting the lack of industry and compulsion to resort to small retail businesses.

Industry observers note that “This is dictatorship,” said Kumar, a staunch Modi supporter until the demolition drive. “And no one raises our voice because the media doesn’t broadcast anything critical of Modi.”.

Industry observers note that about a dozen other upper-caste Hindus in the city who professed to be pro-Modi said the BJP was unlikely to win Meerut even if it retains the state. That could change if there were credible opposition, but they did not see a match. Congress scion Rahul Gandhi marched alongside protesters and promised to seek justice for those wrongfully detained or beaten up. In Delhi, Gen Z protesters spoke in his favor. But in a state deeply divided along caste lines, despite being upper caste, he is still not seen as an alternative.

Akash, a 26-year-old from Bulandshahr, noted that the BJP will return to power because it had ensured quick payment for sugarcane to farmers like his father. “There are also more roads and police stations,” he said, emphasizing improvement in law and order under the BJP government led by Modi acolyte Yogi Adityanath. He said that Indians like him would rate Modi on economic development over the protests in Delhi or the state of Indian democracy. But he also didn’t want to give up his own right to protest or question the government.

“If the choice is between a better economy and democracy, I choose the economy, but if it is between the economy and my ability to question the government, then I choose democracy,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, like Meerut in Uttar Pradesh, in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, local factors were adding to a sense that all was not well under the Modi government. But here, too, the protests were not the reason that people said the government could change. “Farmers are not being paid on time,” Bhawani Singh, a tourist taxi driver, said. “Our children will never go and protest like those in Delhi. But we are upset about the Agnipath scheme and the shortening of military service,” he said, referring to government looks to cut down the length of service below the rank of officer to four years and retain only a quarter for a full term. “Most kids here want to join the army or the police,” he said. (The government appears to have noticed the grievance, announcing earlier this month that two more years of service could be offered and a second chance at joining longer-term,, for those who meet the selection criteria.).

According to recent reports, local factors remain paramount for Indians deciding how Modi has fared in his third term. The protests have had some effect on their overall assessment—distancing those affected by other government policies, while many remain ambivalent or supportive. The weakening of institutions isn’t yet a factor in how they vote, but it has been registered, as former supporters say the media is largely pliable, and now the Election Commission is suspected of being subservient.

Recent findings suggest that the fence-sitters are the upper-caste Hindus who form the backbone of the BJP’s voter base. And while many are still firmly behind the party and backing Hindu dominance, at least some appeared uncomfortable with a slide away from democracy. “He wants to be Putin,” an upper-caste Hindu said  . “Now with the delimitation bill, the BJP is trying to ensure it always has enough seats to keep them in power,” he added, referring to legislation that will come up for voting in parliament next month and intends to expand the number of seats based on population. The same exercise in Jammu and Kashmir, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said, helped the BJP.

The recent protests are occurring in the middle of Modi’s current stint in office. He still has time to assuage concerns. But the opposition will also have a chance to highlight its case about the weakening of democratic institutions and the threat to Indian democracy. And just as a political wave pushed Modi into office 12 years ago, another one could be building that will eventually sweep him out.

Industry observers note that former Southern Poverty Law Center executive Heidi Beirich faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy. The Department of Justice alleges Beirich hid over $4 million in payments from SPLC donors to fund White supremacy.

A former Southern Poverty Law Center official who led its hate-group tracking work told FBI agents he tried to make the watchdog’s controversial "Hate Map" more ideologically balanced, while saying Christians and conservatives were the first staffers pushed out in what he called a "long-term coup" at the organization after he left in 2013.

The former director remarked he pushed for a more evenhanded SPLC, arguing that its "Hate Map" — which lists conservative groups alongside Ku Klux Klan chapters — should also include left-wing extremists, including violent animal-rights and extremist environmental groups. However, the former director said the effort met resistance and that, as liberal leaders reshaped the organization, most of his 17-person team was replaced.

"There was some kind of coup, long-term coup going on there between some, what I would — what I heard were some pretty liberal people, extreme people that had other ideas about what we were doing," the unnamed former director told agents, as first reported by The Daily Signal's Tyler O'Neil, who has been covering the SPLC's legal troubles.

DOJ EXPANDS INDICTMENT AGAINST SPLC, ALLEGING $4M SECRETLY FUNNELED TO KKK AND EXTREMIST GROUPS.

SPLC Intelligence Project Director Heidi Beirich speaks during an event on Jan. 12, 2018. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that the former director’s comments appeared in an FBI interview transcript filed as an exhibit to Dr. Heidi Beirich’s Nov. 2 court filing. Beirich, a former SPLC official charged alongside the organization in a federal case alleging a scheme to mislead donors and banks about donations used to pay informants associated with violent extremist groups, pointed to multiple FBI interviews with an unnamed former SPLC director, identified in the filing as "Individual-1.".

It has been revealed that in a January interview, Individual-1 told investigators he ran the SPLC’s field-source program, set up accounts used to pay sources and directed payments, according to Beirich’s filing. During a March 23 follow-up interview with Individual-1, FBI Special Agents David McDaniel and Parker Still framed the conversation around the program having "gone off the rails" under Beirich and told the former director they were not there to discuss the bank activity, noting he had "obviously nothing to do with all that," before questioning him about the SPLC’s alleged targeting of conservative organizations and Beirich’s role, according to the transcript.

EXCLUSIVE: SPLC'S 'FAR-LEFT,' 'ANTI-RACISM' CURRICULUM FOUND IN CLASSROOMS AS EARLY AS KINDERGARTEN: 'WATCHDOG'.

Individual-1 responded that, as his "gut impression," he believed her actions were political and accused some liberals at the center of having "a good degree of hatred" for conservatism, according to the March 23 transcript.

Industry observers note that individual-1 also alleged a shift in power at the SPLC. After he left in 2013, he stated, people were appointed to the SPLC’s board as "figureheads" and eventually gained enough voting power to take over the center. He said only one or two data-entry members of his roughly 17-person team remained, with the others replaced by staff he believed shared the latest leadership’s politics.

Recent findings suggest that "That's who they ran off first were the Christians and conservatives," the unnamed former director told agents when asked why Beirich took the actions she did after his departure. "Then they — then the rest they just replaced with people they liked, you know, that agreed with them politically.".

HOW MUTINY AT SOUTHERN POVERTY LAW CENTER TRIGGERED LEADERSHIP COLLAPSE.

The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) building seen in March 2020 in Montgomery, Alabama. (Barry Lewis/InPictures via Getty Images).

Sources indicate that in separate comments about the SPLC's controversial "Hate Map," Individual-1 stated he persuaded SPLC staff, despite internal resistance, to list Black separatist groups, which he considered comparable to White racist groups, on the map. However, he said he unsuccessfully pushed the SPLC to include violent animal-rights and environmental extremist groups and described his team’s approach during his tenure as director as "very nonpartisan" and "middle of the road.".

"We were very nonpartisan, or at least when I was running things, when I was director, we stayed right in the middle of the road," he noted.

In a June follow-up, the unnamed former director also criticized the SPLC's "Hate Map" for listing local chapters separately, saying it made the map's totals of the extremist groups it chose to identify look larger.

According to recent reports, while the unnamed former director was not charged in the SPLC case, Beirich was. Her lawyers say the interviews with the unnamed director warrant discovery into whether she was singled out because of her perceived role in the SPLC’s political speech, arguing that investigators’ questions about the SPLC’s treatment of conservative groups — and her alleged role in that work — could show the prosecution was motivated by hostility to the center’s political speech.
